title: The Tea Party
strapline: You're invited: pour the tea, pass the cake, and mind your manners — one lump or two?
intent: A tea party gathers children around a shared table where welcoming, offering, pouring and passing are naturally polite, turn-taking work.
Pouring from a real teapot and passing loaded plates is precise physical work with real consequences for a wobble.
Setting the table — a cup, saucer, plate and spoon for each guest — is honest one-to-one counting and matching.
The ritual of hosting invites rich, courteous conversation: 'would you like some more?', 'thank you, this is delicious'.
A tea party belongs to many cultures and celebrations, so it can host the drinks, sweets and customs of every family in the room.
Small, calm and sociable, it draws in children who find bigger, louder play harder to join.
implementation: Model the host's warmth and script — 'do come and sit down', 'may I pour you some tea?' — until it becomes the children's own.
Use real small teapots and unbreakable china so the pouring is genuinely wet and the trust builds control.
Lay the table together, counting a full setting for each guest and each teddy invited.
Add real (or playdough) treats to pass and share, and let children work out fair shares — 'three of us, three biscuits, how do we do it?'
Invite the teas and sweet things of many homes, and let families share how they take their tea.
Slow it right down — this is play that rewards calm, quiet, courteous attention.
key_questions: May I pour you some tea?
Have we got a cup, saucer and plate for every guest?
Three of us, three biscuits — how do we share them?
Would you like some more? What do you say?
How does your family take their tea at home?

impact.text: Children welcome, offer, pour and pass in naturally polite, turn-taking play.
Children pour from a real teapot and pass loaded plates — precise physical work.
Children set the table, counting a cup, saucer, plate and spoon for each guest — one-to-one matching.
Children host with rich, courteous conversation across several turns.
Children host the drinks, sweets and customs of every family in the room.

enhancements: Real small teapots and unbreakable china so the pouring is genuinely wet.
A full table setting counted and matched for every guest and teddy.
Real or playdough treats to pass, share and work out into fair shares.
The teas and sweet things of many homes, shared by families.
A calm, quiet corner so the play rewards courteous attention.

playing_exploring: Children step into a gentle grown-up ritual and the props — teapot, cups, cake stand — pull them straight into pouring and offering.
They test how full a cup can be poured before it spills, and how to carry a loaded plate steadily.
active_learning: Hosting means holding several courtesies in mind at once — greeting, pouring, offering, sharing — and children rise to it because it matters.
creating_thinking: Children solve the fairness puzzles a shared table throws up — how to split three cakes between four friends.
